text: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Yes, do bear with me.
I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you to Christ as a pure virgin.
But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts may be corrupted and drawn away from the sincerity and purity of your devotion to Christ.

versions.text: But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
versions.explanation: The verb φθαρῇ means "be corrupted/ruined," which is stronger than "led astray." Retaining the idea of corruption preserves the force of Paul's warning while keeping the sentence readable aloud.

versions.text: But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts may be corrupted and drawn away from the sincere and pure devotion that belongs to Christ.
versions.explanation: τῆς εἰς τὸν Χριστόν marks the direction of the believers' sincerity and purity — devotion directed toward Christ — not something belonging to Christ. The phrase "devotion that belongs to Christ" reverses the relationship; the corrected wording keeps the intentional "corrupted" rendering while restoring the sense of the Greek preposition.

text: For if someone comes along preaching another Jesus than the one we preached, or if you receive a different spirit than the one you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it easily enough.
Yet I consider myself in no way inferior to those "super-apostles."
Even if I am untrained as a speaker, I am not lacking in knowledge. We have made this plain to you in every way and in every situation.
Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God's gospel to you free of charge?
I robbed other churches, accepting their support in order to serve you.

And when I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. I have kept myself from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so.
As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows that I do!

versions.text: Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do.
versions.explanation: The Greek is simply "God knows." The added "I do" is a reasonable clarification, but as it stands the sentence reads as if God's knowledge is the object of the previous clause. Punctuating it as its own emphatic statement makes the sense clearer for a listener.

text: And what I am doing I will keep on doing, so as to cut the ground from under those who are looking for a chance to be found our equals in the very thing they boast about.

versions.text: And what I am doing I will keep on doing, in order to cut the ground from under those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things they boast about.
versions.explanation: The current sentence is long and top-heavy for oral reading, and "want an opportunity to be regarded" blurs the Greek's two clauses ("who want an opportunity" and "so that they may be found just as we are"). The revision keeps both ideas distinct and flows better when read aloud.

text: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.
And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.
So it is no surprise if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will match their works.
Again I say: let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then accept me as a fool, so that I too may do a little boasting.
What I am saying now, I am not saying as the Lord would, but as a fool would, in this business of boasting.
Since so many are boasting according to the flesh, I too will boast.
After all, you gladly put up with fools, since you are so wise!
For you put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone puts on airs, if someone slaps you in the face.
To my shame I admit that we were too weak for that! But whatever anyone else dares to boast about—I am speaking as a fool—I dare it too.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham's offspring? So am I.
Are they servants of Christ? I am out of my mind to talk this way—I am more: in far greater labors, in far more imprisonments, in far worse beatings, often at the point of death.

versions.text: Are they servants of Christ? I am out of my mind to talk this way—I am more: in harder labors, in more imprisonments, in far worse beatings, in frequent danger of death.
versions.explanation: περισσοτέρως denotes greater quantity or degree ("far more"), not primarily difficulty, and ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις is more vividly rendered "often at the point of death" than the flat "in frequent danger of death." The parallel "far ... far ... far" also strengthens the oral rhythm of the list.

text: Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes minus one.
Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked; I spent a night and a day adrift at sea.

I have been constantly on the move: in danger from rivers, in danger from bandits, in danger from my own people, in danger from Gentiles, in danger in the city, in danger in the wilderness, in danger at sea, in danger from false brothers.
I have labored and toiled, often gone without sleep; I have known hunger and thirst, often gone without food; I have been cold and without clothing.
And besides everything else, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches.
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not inwardly burn?

versions.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn with grief?
versions.explanation: πυροῦμαι is left deliberately open in Greek (burning with indignation, distress, or grief). Specifying "with grief" narrows the sense; "inwardly burn" preserves the ambiguity and the punch of the rhetorical question.

versions.text: Who is made to stumble, and I do not inwardly burn?
versions.explanation: The first of Paul's two paired rhetorical questions, τίς ἀσθενεῖ, καὶ οὐκ ἀσθενῶ; ("Who is weak, and I am not weak?"), has been dropped from the verse. Restoring it recovers the missing clause and the deliberate parallelism, while keeping the intentionally chosen "inwardly burn" for πυροῦμαι.

text: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.
In Damascus the governor under King Aretas kept the city of the Damascenes under guard in order to arrest me,
but I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and slipped through his hands.
